extracted.intended_audience: government contracting officers, attorneys and advisers handling U.S. federal government contracts
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts legal standards governing assignment, performance, formality, and conflicts-of-interest for contracts with the United States (statutes §3477, §3737, §3744, related Army regulations, and case practice). Aimed at advising contracting officers and counsel on when transfers, payments, receivers, deaths, sureties, and officers' interests affect contracts and claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3737 — assignment of government contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: The transfer of the contract or any interest therein 'shall cause the annulment of the contract so far as the United States is concerned' (section 3737, R. S.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While early authorities treated such assignments as absolutely null and void, later opinions (Attorney General) construe the statute as intended for the benefit and protection of the United States only — the Government may recognize and accept an assignee and pay it. However, an officer of the Army cannot properly treat an assignment as valid without authority and direction from the Secretary of War. The prohibition applies to voluntary transfers and not to those made under judicial proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignments that do not ordinarily constitute prohibited transfers
rubrics_metrics.description: Partnership arrangements and arrangements for financial assistance in connection with a contract will not ordinarily constitute an assignment within the meaning of section 3737.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similarly, a contractor contracting with a third party simply to furnish material for the work does not assign the contract (cases: Hobbs v. McLean; Coates v. U. S.; U. S. v. Farley). Courts examine the substance of relations and intention; mere financial assistance or subcontract-supply relationships are not automatically prohibited assignments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting suggestion for transfer clause in contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the statutory language declares that transfer 'shall cause the annulment of the contract so far as the United States is concerned,' it is better to use a clause stating 'in case of such transfer the United States may refuse to carry out this contract either with the transferor or the transferee' to more clearly express the statute's intent as construed by the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a recommended form of clause to reflect the Government's discretionary remedy rather than an absolute automatic annulment; cited C. 2878, Jan. 19, 1897.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions — involuntary assignments, bankruptcy, receivers, assignments for benefit of creditors
rubrics_metrics.description: Sections 3477 and 3737 do not apply to involuntary assignments in bankruptcy, or to voluntary assignments for the benefit of creditors, or to assignments by order of a State court to a receiver appointed by the State court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there has been an assignment for the benefit of creditors or a court-appointed receiver, payments due or to become due on the contract should be made to the duly appointed assignee/receiver and cannot legally be made to the assignors; Circular and Comptroller opinions cited. Receiver acts as officer of appointing court and stands in place of company.

rubrics_metrics.name: Receiver may perform and bind the contract
rubrics_metrics.description: A receiver duly appointed for a company having a contract with the United States may be permitted to execute the contract; payments being made to the receiver on receipts signed by him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This action is not an assignment prohibited by section 3737 because the receiver is an officer of the court acting under its orders. After appointment, the company cannot exercise acts with reference to its property and contracts. If the receiver declines or fails to perform to an extent permitting the Government to procure the work elsewhere, losses may be charged to the contractor or receiver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment by operation of law (death) — executor/administrator rights and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3737 does not apply to assignment by operation of law: where a party died pending performance, his executor or administrator may complete the contract after filing proof of appointment; but executor/administrator cannot assign the contract to others without violating section 3737.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the contract required personal services (e.g., an artist), the contract terminates on death and cannot be carried out by executor/administrator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction: assignment of contract vs assignment of claim (section 3477)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a manifest distinction between assignment of a Government contract (prohibited by §3737) and an assignment of a claim for money due under the contract (not prohibited if properly made under §3477).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: However, an assignment of claims that is in substance a transfer of the contract (e.g., assignment of all claims with power to collect plus recital that it is 'further continuing collateral security' and a mortgage on property) will be treated as an assignment of the contract within §3737 and invalid. An assignment need not be formal or express; courts look to facts and circumstances indicating intent. §3477 is broad and embraces all claims against the Government; assignments not made as prescribed are declared 'absolutely null and void' as against the Government, but payments actually made to an assignee under an informal/unrevoked power of attorney will be valid as between the parties and accounting officers must allow disbursing officers credit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subrogation / surety payments and limits under §3477 and surety practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a contractor became financially unable to continue and his surety carried on the work and paid debts, upon proof of assignment to it of the contractor's rights the payments due the contractor might be paid to such surety; upon completion retained percentages might be paid the surety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But agreements by a contractor to make the surety subrogated to all rights or to assign deferred payments to the surety were held void as assignments to the surety of any money due from the Government under §3477 (C. 7311, Dec. 28, 1899). The practice must be reconciled with §3477's restrictions on assignments of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Payments and competing claimants — department heads not compelled to arbitrate
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties representing opposing interests cannot, by presenting conflicting claims to a head of a department, compel him to become a stakeholder or arbitrator upon the merits of their demands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The department head should not be forced into adjudicating claims; proper legal remedies apply. Examples show Treasury/accounting doctrine and case law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section 3744 — writing and signature requirement for Government contracts
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3744 prescribes that every contract made by the Secretaries of War, Navy, and Interior (or their officers) shall be reduced to writing and signed by the contracting parties; the statute has been construed as mandatory, equivalent to a statute of frauds, and essential to the validity of contracts with the Government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An acceptance of a bid or letter acceptance by the Government is generally preliminary and does not constitute a binding contract under §3744; performance begun before signing does not convert the preliminary acceptance into a valid written contract, although recovery may be limited to quantum meruit for use. Cases: Clark v. U. S.; South Boston Iron Co. v. U. S. Courts hold the writing requirement mandatory to prevent fraud upon the Treasury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army regulations — officers contracting with persons in military service; waiver and exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: Army Regulations (paragraphs 589, 593, 746, 1002) generally forbid officers or agents in the military service from purchasing from or contracting with other persons in the military service or making contracts where such persons share any part or benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These prohibitions are directed to the officer and may be waived by the Secretary of War in a given case. They do not apply to contracts requiring the Secretary's approval (which the Secretary may authorize), nor always to civilians employed in the public service under the War Department. A contract with an incorporated company in which an officer holds stock is not necessarily barred. Where facts show the spouse's business is her separate enterprise (wife of soldier), the prohibition may not apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest — Members of Congress and sureties (sections 3739–3742)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under §§3739–3742 R. S., it is illegal for an officer of the United States to contract for or purchase for the United States any supplies from a Member or Delegate to Congress or from a firm (other than an incorporated company) in which such Member or Delegate is a member or pecuniarily interested.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These sections do not forbid acceptance of a Member or Delegate as surety on a bond, but acceptance is discouraged because surety subrogation could create contractual relations between the United States and a Member of Congress; recommendation that a Member of Congress not be accepted as surety (C. 14923, July 6, 1903). Note later Federal Penal Code provisions may broaden application to time of election.
